name: 1st Apron, Left Side
text: [overview] Slab climbing hugging the glacier on the first Apron, whose face points ENE, about 30 minutes WSW of the Summit Lake parking.

name: 2nd Apron Left Side
text: [overview] Start on angling cracks by the snow tongue, trend left under a little roof, then work through 500-600 ft of fractured rock at 5.6, some 5.7, to a grassy terrace.

name: 2nd Apron Right Side
text: [overview] Snow can linger at the foot, and lightning and other mountain hazards apply.

name: Amphitheater Route (aka Fowler Memorial Route)
text: [overview] Waterfall ice pitches are separated by easy snow and alpine ice.
[detailed_rack] Roughly four or five screws, a pair of ropes, and possibly a picket (?).
[descent_text] Easy alpine ice and snow separate the waterfall pitches, which matters if you need to downclimb or rappel.

name: Portland Creek
text: [descent_text] From the top, walk off west and either find a hidden chute into the larger northwest-facing gully (only with high snow) or rappel into the same gully.

name: North Face Direct
text: [overview] Past the apron it narrows and forks at 500 feet: left climbs snow that is very steep, or easy ice;
[overview] right leads to a bigger snowfield, from which to cross back left over the rib.
[overview] 400 feet of moderate snow leads to a second fork.
[overview] Left, a brief pitch of ice or mixed climbing of unknown difficulty, then snow to a summit headwall whose exit might be challenging.
[overview] Right, after 300 feet, a rim that is steep and possibly corniced reaches the ridge west of the summit.
[what_to_bring] crampons.
[approach] Snow may stop vehicles short of the trailhead in the colder months, lengthening the walk.

name: Andrews Glacier
text: [overview] A well-known landmark that is possibly the sole non-technical glacier in the Park at certain times of year.
[overview] Late summer and fall turn it to alpine ice, so crampons are advisable, and once snow has fallen, avalanches can be a hazard.
[overview] In winter the surface may be soft snow or hard wind crust, at a steeper angle overall.
[overview] Later in the season, the left (south) edge may allow bypassing the snow, reportedly tricky depending on melt-out.
[detailed_rack] Pickets are a good choice if protection is needed.

name: Box of Candy Couloir
text: [approach] Begin at the Glacier Gorge trailhead and walk toward Andrews Glacier.
[approach] At Andrews Tarn, near the foot of the glacier, climb up the glacier while trending to the left.
[approach] The couloir hugs the rock wall on that side, and you are at its start when a snow, ice and rock ramp heads south.
[approach] Small crevasses near the bottom of the glacier can be deep, so take care around them.
[descent_text] Hike over to Andrews Glacier, descend it, and rejoin the main trail back to the trailhead.

name: Brain Freeze
text: [approach] From the Glacier Gorge trailhead, follow the trail to The Loch and continue a little farther to the log bridge over Andrews Creek, where a sign points to Andrews Glacier.
[approach] In the snowy months this trail is lightly used and can be hard to follow;
[approach] It curves left and opens up to the south face of Otis Peak, with Andrews Glacier off to the west.
[approach] The Gash is the basin just south (left) of the glacier, ending at the spire of Sharkstooth.
[descent_text] The snow gully just west of the route is another way down and leads straight to the base.

name: Chiropractic Couloir
text: [overview] A curving snow couloir that stands out in spring and can be seen from the town below.
[overview] A huge cornice at the top holds into early May, and snow has mostly melted by early June.
[overview] Moving fast on a cold morning and leaving left near the upper end avoids the cornice.
[overview] Should the cornice release partway up and take a climber off their feet, a cliff of 50 feet below is the risk.
[detailed_rack] Pickets, a few rock pieces, or both can protect it.
[approach] From the Glacier Gorge side, follow the route toward Andrews Glacier and turn left into The Gash, the hanging valley between the glacier and Sharkstooth.
[approach] These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
[descent_text] The couloir ends on the ridge above a broad, fan-shaped headwall, and a large cornice often guards the top into spring.
[descent_text] Exiting left avoids the cornice.
[descent_text] From the crest, turn north (right) to Andrews Glacier and descend it to the Andrews Glacier trail.
[descent_text] The glacier is a snow slope that firms up to ice late in the year, so carry an axe and crampons.

[approach] The line sits between Zowie and Wham on Otis Peak's south side, and starts with steps kicked up gully snow into a sheltered cave under the first chockstone.

text: [overview] The upper section is steepest, where the couloir broadens to a large snowfield, possibly past 60 degrees;
[overview] The season is short: it faces south with a big upper snowfield, so it is avalanche prone early and melted out later.
[detailed_rack] Only pickets could protect the steep upper snowfield.
[approach] From the Glacier Gorge trailhead, follow the trail to The Loch and continue a little farther to the log bridge over Andrews Creek, where a sign points to Andrews Glacier.

[approach] The Gash is the basin just south (left) of the glacier, ending at the spire of Sharkstooth.
[approach] It faces south and a big snowfield sits above it, so it is prone to slides early in the season.

name: Northwest Gully of Sharkstooth
text: [overview] A winter snow climb on Sharkstooth's west flank, viewed from The Gash, brief yet steep.
[detailed_rack] Well suited to soloing, though pickets or a lightweight rock rack can protect it.
[approach] Follow the Andrews Glacier route toward Andrews Tarn and turn left into The Gash, heading for Sharkstooth.
[approach] These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

name: Andrews' Tower, North Face
text: [overview] Begin on the rocky ground separating the snowfield below from Andrews Glacier, by Tarn Lake.
[overview] Pitch 1 (M3-4, 200'): mixed snow and rock.
[overview] Pitch 3 (M4): very steep snow beneath the cornice, then at the headwall go hard left to the arete.
[overview] Pitch 4: turn right along the mostly snowy ridge to the col.
[detailed_rack] screws and pickets are not needed.

name: Queen's Way
text: [overview] A route up Apache by way of the Isabelle Glacier, entering from the head of the South Saint Vrain valley.

[approach] From the Brainard Lake area start at the Long Lake trailhead and follow the Pawnee Pass trail past Long Lake to Lake Isabelle, then continue west along the Isabelle Glacier trail to the tarn below Navajo, Apache and Shoshoni peaks.
[approach] Cross the Isabelle Glacier to its southwest corner, where the route climbs a steep snow ramp to a saddle below the summit.
[approach] These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

name: Arapaho Peaks Traverse
text: [overview] A good trail leads to South Arapaho, then a sustained, exposed Class 3 ridge with a brief Class 4 crux leads north above the Arapaho Glacier.
[beta] Trail to South Arapaho: follow the Arapaho Pass trail to the Fourth of July Mine ruins, then switch back northeast on the signed Arapaho Glacier trail.
[beta] the east side drops to the glacier.
[beta] Final slopes: easier ground, sometimes with a lingering snow patch, leads to North Arapaho's broad summit.
[obj_haz] Steep drop-offs on the glacier side
[watch_out] The Arapaho Glacier basin east of the ridge is Boulder's watershed and closed to all entry

[approach] Turn sharply back to the northeast onto the signed Arapaho Glacier trail and follow it above treeline to the saddle on South Arapaho's southeast shoulder (about 12,700 ft), then scramble to South Arapaho's summit (about 4 mi from the trailhead).
[descent_text] Reverse the traverse south to South Arapaho, then descend the Arapaho Glacier trail and Arapaho Pass trail back to the trailhead.
[descent_text] Descending the east side of the ridge toward the glacier is not an option: that basin is closed to all entry.
[bail] do not try to descend east toward the glacier, which is steep, loose and closed to entry.
[pitch_detail] Arapaho Pass trail to the mine ruins, Arapaho Glacier trail to the saddle, then a loose rocky scramble past a false summit to the top..
[pitch_detail] Scramble off South Arapaho to the saddle, then follow the Arapaho Glacier trail and the Arapaho Pass trail back down past the mine ruins..

name: Skywalker Couloir
text: [detailed_rack] An occasional picket may help, and some gear fits in the couloir walls.

name: Streetwalker Couloir
text: [overview] A couloir of easy to moderate snow, not nearly as classic as the famous one next door, and similar to the lower part of the neighboring Skywalker.
[overview] Once roughly 1000' of snow is behind you, get past a band of rock on its right side, then aim west for South Arapahoe's summit.
[detailed_rack] For belaying, two pickets or so and a small selection of rock gear should be enough.
[approach] Streetwalker is the rightmost finger of snow, about 200 yards right of Skywalker.
[approach] It resembles the lower part of Skywalker, with easy to moderate snow.
[approach] These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.

text: [approach] Scramble around the north side of the lake beneath the east face and aim for North Chimney, the hidden gully below the middle of the Diamond with a snow tongue reaching into it;
[approach] North Chimney is loose fourth and low fifth class (about 5.4) with snow early in the season, so keep out from under other parties and expect rockfall.

text: [approach] From the Glacier Gorge lot, take the trail to Sky Pond.
[approach] After the Andrews Glacier trail junction and before the climb to the waterfall, leave the trail and traverse the talus slopes to the wall.
[descent_text] All the routes on this wall top out in the same area, and the walk-off goes down the back to the Andrews Glacier trail.
[descent_text] The Gash gives access to the Andrews Glacier basin, and from there a walk around the shoulder leads back.

name: Central Buttress
text: [overview] Descent, fastest: 20 minutes north on the Continental Divide, then Andrews Glacier and Andrews Creek.
[overview] Alternatively walk ten minutes to the North Gully, downclimb its first 100' (steep snow), then descend 800' by plunge-stepping to the base snowfield.

name: Chimney Sweep
text: [overview] Takes the middle of the face over the snow tongue, left of the big central rib.
[overview] Ascend the stiff snow of the main couloir, then scramble 300 feet of terraces to the center crack.

name: Cold Blooded Boys
text: [overview] Approach: follow the trail up Glacier Gorge to Green Lake, climb the North Gully that separates Pagoda Mountain from the Keyboard of the Winds to sit below Sievers' Tower, then cross east beneath the Keyboards.

name: South Face
text: [overview] Depending on the year, possibly the gentlest, most secure line up the peak: tidy scrambling plus moderate snow in place of the northwest gully's ice and rubble.

name: Alpine Ambition
text: [detailed_rack] A picket may help, since many cruxes begin on steep snow that is firm, with scant protection before several insecure moves.

name: Grendel's Lair
text: [approach] The usual way in follows that drainage, which is steep, brushy and slow, and in a dry early winter it can be mostly free of snow.
[approach] The ice starts as a low notch at the foot of the Northwest Couloir and grows down toward the snowfield below.
[descent_text] Once down at the steep snow ramp above the first pitch, stroll down and around the gentle snowfield back to the foot of the climb.

[descent_text] A walk-off is also possible from the top: leave the notch and go left over the diamond-shaped wall, which is snowy third-class ground that is best done with plenty of daylight or route-finding experience.

name: Ptarmigan Song
text: [overview] Follow steep snow up the gully about one rope length to an exit gully that breaks right from the main one.
[overview] Mixed climbing through that exit gully gives access to the adjacent gully, which runs to the summit across moderate snow and ice runnels totaling 1500'.
[approach] Overhangs cap both walls of the dihedral, but a line of ice slips between them to a choke below a moderate snow slope.
[approach] Do not follow the obvious snow line that ends at a gap in the ridge to the summit's west;

name: Diamond Couloir
text: [approach] Its neighbours are the broad snowfield to the left and the First Apron to the right.
[approach] These are steep snow slopes in avalanche terrain, so check the avalanche forecast first.
[descent_text] Follow the snow as it steepens up to the cliff band where it stops, then keep left (east) of the steep rock and take a couple of Class 4 steps up to the west ridge.
[descent_text] In good snow cover the couloir is also skied back to Summit Lake.
[descent_text] Crampons and an axe are the norm, and a rope is optional for the Class 4 ground.

name: Dicker's Peck
text: [overview] A pinnacle in the notch to the north of Navajo, visible while hiking the trail up Isabel Glacier.
[overview] Reach the notch by a snow route, the most direct being Navajo Snowfield at 45 degrees, or by the East Ledges line on Apache, once it has melted out.
[overview] Descend by scrambling to Navajo's summit and down the loose Airplane gully, which holds an old plane wreck and returns to where the snow climbs begin.
